Wretch that I am, what strains of woe break from me!
O that some bird, high on the waving bough
Of oak or fir, her mother lost, would join
Her griefs to mine, and echo back my notes
In harmony of sorrow, wailing thus
These gaping wounds! For ever shall I lead
A solitary life, for ever wail
As now, the tears still streaming from mine eyes.
To whom, whom first shall I devote these locks
Rent from my head? Where shall I offer them?
Lay them upon my mother's breasts of milk,
Or on the deep wounds of my slaughter'd brothers -
Come forth, my aged father, leave thy house,
Bringing thy sightless eye; show, Edipus,
Thy wretched age, thou, that within the house,
Darkling amidst the gloom thine own hands wrought,
Dost drag a ling'ring life. Hear'st thou my voice,
Dark-wand'ring in thy hall, or on thy couch
Resting thy age-enfeebled weary foot?
Why, virgin, with these lamentable cries
Why hast thou brought my blind, staff-guided steps,
Call'd from my couch within my darksome chamber
To light, a grey and unsubstantial phantom,
A body from the tomb, a fleeting dream ?

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Unhappy are the tidings, O my father,
Which thou shalt hear. Thy sons no more behold
The light of heav'n: thy wife no more, whose care
With constant tenderness beside thy staff
Supported thy dark steps. Alas, my father!
Alas, my miseries! For to groan, to wail
These things is yet allow'd me. By what fate,
These three, how left they this ethereal light?
Tell me, my child.
I mean not to reproach,
I mean not to insult; but with deep sorrow
1 speak: thy evil genius, O my father,

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Hurtling with swords, and fire, and ruthless combats,
Wherefore these groans!
Rush'd on thy sons.

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: Ah me! unhappy me!

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: My sons!
The paths indeed

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: Of sorrow wou'dst thou tread, if by the car
Of yon refulgent sun illumed thine eyes
Might o'er these lifeless bodies roll their orbs.
The ruin of my sons needs not a comment :
But my unhappy wife, by what ill fate,
Tell me, my child, am I deprived of her ?

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Her mournful tears fast-streaming in the sight
Of all, before her sons she bared her breast,
Suppliant she bared her breast in suppliant guise.
Before th' Electran gates, where with the lotus
The mead abounds, her sons the mother found
Contending with their spears, like two young lions
Bred in one cave, whilst from their gaping wounds
The kindred gore outwell'd; for now had Mars
Presented that libation, bloody, cold,
And Pluto had receiv'd it. From the dead
She snatch'd the sword, and plung'd the ruthless blade
Deep in her body: nigh her sons she fell,
In death embracing each. This day, my father,
The god, that wrought these things, hath crush'd our house
With all th' accumulated weight of woe.

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: This day hath to the house of Edipus
Been the beginning of unnumber'd woes.
May the succeeding days bring happier fortune!

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: No more of lamentation, as the time

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: Calls our attention to the funeral rites.
Now hear me, Edipus, and mark my words.
To me thy son Eteocles assign'd
The sceptre of this land, the nuptial dowery
To Hæmon with the bed of this thy daughter

sp.speaker: Antigone
sp.l: No longer then will I
Permit thee to inhabit here: full clearly
Tiresias spoke, that whilst thou dwellest in it
This city should not flourish: quit it then:
I speak not this t' insult thee; nor am I
Thine enemy: but thy avenging demons
I dread, lest aught of ill the state should suffer.
O fate, how wretched, how oppress'd with ills,
Such as man never suffer'd, hast thou form'd me
E'en from my birth! Me, e'er I saw the light
Of life, the voice of Phœbus from his shrine
Declared the future murderer of my father,
Wretch that I am! Soon as I breath'd this air,
Laius, who gave me life, to death assign'd me,
As an ill-fated foe, beneath whose hand
It was his destiny to die; a prey
To savage beasts my wretched infancy
Craving the breast he cast forth; yet from thence
Was I preserv'd: O had Cithæron sunk
Down to the yawning gulfs of Tartarus,
Which did not then destroy me! As a slave
To Polybus the ruthless pow'r assign'd me.
Ill-fated wretch, I slew my father, mounted
My mother's hapless bed, and begot sons
My brothers: these have I destroy'd, from Laius
The curse receiving, and transmitting it
Down to my sons; for nature form'd me not
So senseless, to devise such stern designs
'Gainst these poor sightless eyes, 'gainst my sons' lives,
But by some god impelling. Be it so.
What then, unhappy, shall I do? What guide
Will my dark steps accompany? Will she,
That here lies dead? Well know I, were she living,
She would attend me.
Will that noble pair,
My sons? I have no sons.
My youthful vigour,
Will that procure me the supports of life?
But whence? Why, Creon, wilt thou kill me thus?
For thou wilt kill me, if thou drive me forth.
Yet shall I not, by groveling at thy knees,
Show my self abject; no inglorious deed
Shall stain the splendor of my former honours.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: Well hast thou said, thou wilt not grasp my knees;
This land I would not suffer thee inhabit.
Now for these bodies: that behoves us bear
Within the royal house: but him, who came
With banded pow'rs to lay his country waste,
Forth from the borders of this injured land
Cast him unburied. To the sons of Thebes
Be this proclaim'd; Whoever shall be found
Crowning his corse, or covering it with earth,
He dies for his offence: No; let him lie
Unwept, unburied, to the birds a prey.
But thou, Antigone, forbear thy grief
For these three dead; retire within the house;
Think what becomes a virgin, and expect
Th' approaching day, when Hæmon's bed awaits thee.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: To what a wretched fortune are we fallen,
Alas, my father! More for thee I mourn,
Than for the dead: thine are not partial ills
Inwoven with good, but one sad scene of woe.
Yet let me ask thee, our new lord, Why thus
With insults drive my father from this land ?

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: Why 'gainst th' unhappy dead pronounce this sentence ?
It is not mine: Eteocles so will'd.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Unwise in him: unwise in thee t' obey.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: Is it not just to execute commands?

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: No, if they 'are ill, and giv'n through ranc'rous hate.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: Is it not just to cast him to the dogs?

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Such vengeance hath the sanction of no law.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: What, though his country's foe, which least became him?

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: To his ill fortune paid he not his life!

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: Ay: and let vengeance wait his out-cast corse.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: What the offence to claim his share of empire ?

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: This man, be well assured, shall lie unburied.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: I, though the state forbid, will bury him.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: Thy self then near his body wilt thou bury.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: 'Tis glorious for two friends to lie together.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: Lay hold on her, and bear her to her chamber.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Off; touch me not; I will not quit this body.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: Fate hath decreed what appears harsh to thee.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: It is decreed the dead be not insulted.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: That o'er his corse none lays the humid earth.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: By my dead mother, by Jocasta, Creon-

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: Thy pray'rs are vain: thou canst not here prevail.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Permit me this at least, to bathe his body.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: This too is interdicted by the state.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Yet let me seemly bind his cruel wounds.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: No honour, Virgin, may'st thou show his body.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Yet, dearest brother, will I kiss thy lips.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: Bear not this ominous mourning to thy nuptials.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: What, whilst I live, shall I e'er wed thy son?
Of strong necessity: how shun his bed?
That night shall find me sprung from Danaus.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: Mark her bold spirit: with what contempt she speaks!

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: The conscious sword be witness to my oath.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: And wherefore dost thou wish to shun these nuptials ?

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: With my unhappy father will I fly.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: 'Tis generous of thee; but there's folly in it.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Wou'dst thou know more? I will e'en die with him.

sp.speaker: Cre
sp.l: Hence then: thou shalt not kill my son: begone.

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: This ready zeal, my child, demands my praise.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: A bride, whilst my poor father strays alone!

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: Remain thou blest: my own ills will I cherish.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Who then shall to thy blindness minister?
Where'er my fate to fall, there will I lie.
Where now is Œdipus ? His honours where?

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: Sunk: one day saw my glory, and my ruin.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Ought I not then to share thy miseries?
To stray an exile with an eyeless father
Is to a daughter shameful.

sp.speaker: Ed
sp.l: To the proud
It may; but not to humble modesty.
Lead me then nearer: let me touch thy mother.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: There: with thy hand touch her most dear remains.
O wretched mother! O most wretched wife!
In this sad state, crush'd with her ills, she lies.
Where lies Eteocles? Polynices where?
In death together stretch'd they lie before thee.
Guide my blind hand to their unhappy faces.
There; as I guide thy hand, touch thy dead sons.

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: Ye wretched ruins of a wretched father!

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: O Polynices, name most dear to me!

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: Now, daughter, is the oracle fulfill'd.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: What? Hast thou more of ills to add to ills?
That wand'ring exiled I should die at Athens.
What citadel of Athens shall receive thee?

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: Colonus, sacred to th' Equestrian god.
But come, to thy blind father be assistant,
Since 'tis thy wish to share his hapless flight.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Go then to hapless flight: reach thy dear hand,
My aged father; take me for thy guide,
A fav'ring gale to waft thy shatter'd bark.

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: I go, my child: be thou my wretched leader.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Wretched indeed we are; Thebes hath no virgin
So very wretched.

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: Which way shall I set
My aged foot? Reach me my staff, my child.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: This way, come this way with me: this way, this way
Advance thy foot, my father, thy worn strength

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: Weak as the phantom of a sickly dream.
O miserable exile! Woe is me!
In mine old age he drives me from my country;
Alas, my suff'rings!
Dwell not on thy suff'rings:
Justice regards not, nor with vengeful hand
Chastises the oppressor's insolence.
Yet reach'd I that sublime and heav'nly lore,
Which led to glorious conquest, when I solved
The dark enigma of the virgin Sphinx.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Why dost thou mention her disgrace? No more
Speak of thy former glories: suff'rings now,
And miseries wait thee, O my father, driv'n
An exile from thy country far to die.
With tears of fond affection tow'rds the virgins
My dear companions, with thee will I go
Far from my country, wand'ring in sad state
Unseemly to a virgin.

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: Generous spirit!

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: That spirit in my father's wretchedness
Shall make me noble. Yet my heart is rent
At this indecent insult on my brother,
Cast out to moulder, an unburied corse.
Him in the secret earth these hands, my father,
Though certain death await me, shall entomb.
Go shew thee to thy friendly train of virgins.
I have enough of wailings.

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: At the altars
Present thy vows.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: They are e'en now o'erloaded
With my afflictions.

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: To the mountains go,
Where unapproach'd, save by the Mænades,
Bacchus his temple holds.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Once on those heights

sp.speaker: Œd
sp.l: Clad in the Theban dress, a fawn's light skin,
I led the sacred dance of Semele :
An unrequited honour to the gods.
Illustrious citizens of Thebes, my country,
Behold your Œdipus, whose piercing mind
Solv'd the mysterious charm, and crush'd the pow'r
Of the blood-ravening Sphinx, the greatest then
Amongst you: now unhonour'd, wretched, driv'n
An out-cast from your land!-But why in vain
Lament I thus and wail, since mortal man
Must bear the hard necessity of fate!

sp.speaker: Chor
sp.l: O Victory, I revere thy sober pow'r:
Guard thou my life, nor ever cease to crown me!
